prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: EN · Long headers, short data (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 5 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 13px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Region" · longest unbreakable word 44px · one-line width 44px
  col 2: header "Quarterly revenue (USD, millions)" · longest unbreakable word 60px · one-line width 212px
  col 3: header "Year-over-year growth rate" · longest unbreakable word 45px · one-line width 172px
  col 4: header "Number of active enterprise customers" · longest unbreakable word 67px · one-line width 248px
  col 5: header "Net promoter score" · longest unbreakable word 59px · one-line width 124px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 619px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 618px.
Fixed: content, font, 13px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 619px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Compare regional commercial performance across revenue, growth, enterprise customers and customer sentiment.","reading":"Readers scan each region across a row, then compare individual measures down their columns. The short body values leave room for headers to wrap without disrupting the data rows.","groups":["Revenue and year-over-year growth describe financial performance.","Enterprise customer count and net promoter score describe the customer base and its sentiment.","Region identifies each row and anchors comparisons across all four measures."],"keep_intact":["Region names and abbreviations","Numeric values, percentages and other individual data values","Whole words in headers"],"may_wrap":["Long headers can wrap at word boundaries; their shared header row can accommodate multiple lines."]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[65,145,125,160,123],"idea":"Balance space across the four measures, giving the longest customer-count header the most room while keeping a compact region column."},{"name":"B","widths":[65,125,110,200,118],"idea":"Prioritize the exceptionally long enterprise-customer header, accepting more wrapping in the revenue and growth headers."},{"name":"C","widths":[65,171,145,137,100],"idea":"Give revenue and growth generous widths for financial scanning, allowing the customer-count and sentiment headers to wrap more."}]}
